The FPC Staff has reviewed available literature and believes that the following bird species in the undetermined category may exist in the proposed project sharp-shinned hawk (Accipiter striatus), Cooper's hawk (A. Cooperii), red-shouldered hawk (Buteo lineatus), osprey (Pandion haliaetus), Swainson's warbler (limnothlypis swainsonii), saw-whet owl (Aegolius acadicus), common raven (Corvus corvax), and the black-capped chickadee (Parus atricapillus). The golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos), classed as rare on the North Carolina list and as an occasional visitor in the mountains, could be observed in the Bad Creek area. Mammals that could also be expected to range into the area and listed by North Carolina as rare include the southeastern myotis (Myotis austroriparius mumfordi), Indiana bat (M. sødalis), masked shrew (Sorex cinereus), smoky shrew (S. fumeus), and the wood rate (neotoma floridana haematoreia).
The bluehead chub (Nocomis leptocephalus interocularis), roseyface chub (Hybopsis rubrifrons), redeye bass (Micropterus coosae), and the turquoise darter (Etheostoma inscriptum) are four fish species listed as peripheral-undetermined, at the edge of their natural range and possibly rare, endangered, or undetermined in North Carolina, but not necessarily elsewhere. One bluehead chub was found in Howard Creek by Applicant in the course of a trout study of Howard Creek in 1975 (Appendix K, exhibit W). The other species are not specifically known for the area, but they could possibly be found within the proposed project area or adjacent region.
Amphibians and reptiles of the Bad Creek area are a combination of mountain and piedmont forms, many of which could be at the edge of their range (Applicant's Exhibit W). The Jordan's Salmander (Plethodon jordani) is listed by Dr. Byron Ingram, Clemson University herpetologist and one of Duke's consultants, as common in the project area, although no population estimate has been made (Applicant's Exhibit W). The Jordan's salmander is restricted to moist forested regions, usually on north-facing slopes (Exhibit W, Appendix C), and small habitat alterations could have an adverse impact on this salamander's populations. The clemsonae variant of the Jordan's salamander, once thought to be found only in the Bad Creek project area, is no longer recognized as a subspecies. It and other variants are considered as only color phases (Conant, 1975). Therefore, the concerns expressed in the Bad Creek Draft Environmental Impact Statement are no longer relevant.
